column1: # Recorded provenance caveats that no automated assurance class can express.
# Read by tools/provenance-inventory.sh.
# A NOTE IS A CAVEAT, NEVER AN ASSURANCE CLASS. Notes are not added to the
# per-class counts and they do not raise or lower a source's class. They exist
# because some facts about a source are true, material, and invisible to every
# check: a build recipe that rewrites upstream's own files, or a signature that
# verifies against a key upstream never designated as its signer.
# Columns are whitespace separated; the note runs to the end of the line.
#   package   the source name, as in tools/fetch-sources.sh and sources.lock
#   kind      recipe-transformation | undesignated-signer
#   location  one token: a path with line numbers, or the URL consulted
#   note      what was found, and what would remove it
# The kinds mean:
#   recipe-transformation   the build recipe modifies or replaces files from
#                           the upstream tarball, and the result is compiled
#                           into what ships. sources.lock therefore does not
#                           fully describe what the artefact was built from.
#   undesignated-signer     a signature verifies, but upstream publishes no
#                           statement about who is authorised to sign its
#                           releases, so the chain stops short of an
#                           authorised signer even when the key is attested.
# A note whose package is not in the manifest is refused: a stale caveat is
# worse than none, because it describes something that is not being shipped.
# Add a kind only together with a row that needs it, and say here what it
# means.
# package  kind                   location                                note

bc         recipe-transformation  build/stages/04-base-system.sh:566-580  s_bc() overwrites upstream's bc/fix-libmath_h with a locally authored sed script. Its output, libmath.h, is compiled into the shipped binary, so sources.lock does not fully describe what bc was built from. The recipe documents and justifies this, and verifies the result functionally (bc -l must evaluate s(0)), but the replacement file is in no lockfile. GNU bc 1.08 makes exactly this change upstream as bc/fix-libmath.sed, so moving the pin would remove the transformation rather than merely hide it.

expat      undesignated-signer    https://libexpat.github.io/             The release signature verifies against primary key 3176EF7DB2367F1FCA4F306B1F9B0E909AF37285, which gentoo.org's Web Key Directory publishes over HTTPS for sping@gentoo.org - a route that does not depend on the signature, so this is NOT circular trust. What is missing is upstream's own statement: libexpat designates no release signer and publishes no fingerprint on its site, in SECURITY.md, or in its release notes. Verified absent on 2026-09-11.

linux-firmware  recipe-transformation  build/stages/04-base-system.sh:s_firmware  The files build/config/firmware.list selects are stored zstd-compressed under /lib/firmware and the kernel decompresses them on load, so the bytes on the verified root are not the tarball's bytes (their decompressed content is). Shipping them uncompressed would remove this.

libnl      undesignated-signer    https://github.com/thom311/libnl/releases  The release tarball carries a detached .sig that verifies against 67DA3FAEBAE276BA58FC6CE314F18A98993AECD5, but libnl publishes no statement of who signs its releases: not on the release page, not in the repository, and the key is in no Web Key Directory. Checked 2026-09-19. A published fingerprint from upstream would remove this.

wpa-supplicant  undesignated-signer  https://w1.fi/wpa_supplicant/  The release tarball carries a detached .asc that verifies against EC4AA0A991A5F2464582D52D2B6EF432EFC895FA (Jouni Malinen), but w1.fi publishes no fingerprint on the download page and the key is in no Web Key Directory for j@w1.fi. Checked 2026-09-19. A published fingerprint from upstream would remove this.

intel-microcode  undesignated-signer  https://github.com/intel/Intel-Linux-Processor-Microcode-Data-Files/releases  Intel publishes its microcode as a GitHub repository whose release tags are lightweight and unsigned, with no detached signature and no published checksum, so sources.lock is the whole of its provenance. The blobs themselves are signed by Intel and the CPU refuses one that is not, which protects the processor and says nothing about which release Kryptik fetched. Checked 2026-09-19.
